The stepwise settlement of the Pacific has left Polynesian communities with variants that are locally common and globally rare. Yet these communities remain underrepresented in genomic research. Here we combine whole-genome sequencing with blood metabolite and gene-activity profiling in a gout-focused cohort of 1,043 French Polynesian participants, and show that such variants shape molecular traits and disease risk. Hundreds alter metabolite levels, gene expression or splicing but are absent or rare in global reference datasets. Findings include a gene-disrupting variant in ANGPTL8 that lowers lipids and inflammatory markers; an LRMDA variant linked to type 2 diabetes; and a signal at the alpha-globin locus suggestive of thalassemia trait. Integrating molecular and phenotypic data further implicates WDR1 as an additional causal gout gene at the SLC2A9 locus. Genomic research in underrepresented populations thus reveals broadly relevant disease mechanisms.

items.title: Recommendation system-inspired learning of crossmodal interaction patterns between chromatin accessibility and gene expression.
items.last_author_affiliation: Data Science and Analytics Thrust, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China. yongqizhang@hkust-gz.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Despite the growing availability of crossmodal single-cell sequencing, existing approaches are limited by underutilization of biological attributes, sparse modality signals, and insufficient modeling of regulatory interactions, limiting generalization in data-scarce settings and the discovery of peak-gene-level relationships. Interestingly, such challenges mirror those in recommendation systems, where side information, high sparsity, binary interactions, and cold start problems are extensively studied. Inspired by recommender models that infer user-item preferences from incomplete interaction graphs, we present CrossRec, which reformulates scATAC and scRNA data as an interaction graph to learn regulatory patterns across single-cell tasks. Its biologically-driven bipartite graph transformer learns interpretable attention over ATAC-RNA pairs. CrossRec outperforms existing methods across various tasks, remains robust under data-scarce settings, generalizes to unseen cell types and datasets, and enhances prior-based methods. Its learned regulatory maps provide cell- and cell-type-specific insights, resolving dynamic regulatory rewiring during cortical neurogenesis and perturbation-specific rewiring of drug-induced regulation in melanoma resistance.

items.title: Phylogenomics of captured Cryptosporidium sequenced directly from patient samples identifies clade-specific genomic architecture and host-adapted lineages.
items.last_author_affiliation: Molecular Parasitology Section, Laboratory of Parasitic Diseases, National institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA. griggm@niaid.nih.gov.
items.abstract: Cryptosporidium causes diarrhea and high mortality in young children in Africa and southern Asia. Low oocyst counts in stool often limit whole-genome sequencing from clinical samples. Here, we enrich for Cryptosporidium genomic DNA directly from stool samples using 74,973 RNA baits (CryptoCap_75K; 8.2 Mb) derived from gene-rich areas (100% coding capacity) within the Cryptosporidium parvum genome. This method produces genome-wide sequence data with sufficient depth and breadth of coverage using as few as 25 oocysts, including divergent species such as Cryptosporidium ubiquitum. To minimize reference bias, we utilize a dual-mapping strategy that integrates reads aligned to both C. parvum and C. ubiquitum to capture lineage-specific variation. Phylogenetic networks, haplotypes, and admixture analyses identify three C. ubiquitum groups, A and B exclusive to humans, with B showing evidence of admixture, whereas C is zoonotic. Group-specific polymorphisms cluster within discrete genomic regions, suggesting conserved haploblocks associate with host adaptation. This capture-based genomics approach provides high-resolution insights into Cryptosporidium population genetics and lays the groundwork for studies of zoonotic transmission, anthroponosis, and GWAS directly from clinical material.

items.title: The nucleolar deubiquitinase OTUD4 coordinates spatial organization of perinucleolar heterochromatin to restrain tumor immunogenicity.
items.last_author_affiliation: Tongji University Cancer Center, Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital, School of Medicine, Tongji University, Shanghai, China. wangp@tongji.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Subnuclear compartmentalization is a foundational determinant of transcriptional homeostasis and cell fate. The nucleolus serves as a scaffold for specialized heterochromatin, yet the mechanisms orchestrating their spatial assembly in malignant contexts remain elusive. Here we identify the nucleolar deubiquitinase OTUD4 as a key regulator of perinucleolar heterochromatin architecture in tumor cells. Casein kinase II (CK2)-mediated phosphorylation activates OTUD4 to specifically remove K63-linked ubiquitin chains from nucleophosmin (NPM1) at lysine 27. This deubiquitination is indispensable for stabilizing the pentameric NPM1 structural scaffold, thereby anchoring H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin to nucleolus. Disruption of the CK2-OTUD4-NPM1 axis in tumor cells triggers heterochromatin detachment, eliciting nucleolar stress and retroelement derepression. This topological collapse activates cytosolic DNA-sensing pathways to potentiate tumor-intrinsic immunogenicity. Clinically, an OTUD4-nucleolus gene signature correlates with adverse survival and immunotherapy resistance in patients with cancer. Collectively, targeting this signal-responsive spatial architecture offers a therapeutic strategy to overcome immune evasion in refractory malignancies.

items.title: Gut epithelial aryl hydrocarbon receptor deficiency aggravates fungal dysbiosis-mediated neutrophilic allergic airway disease in mice.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Surgery, Division of Immunotherapy, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, USA. zhongbin.deng@louisville.edu.; Brown Cancer Center, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, USA. zhongbin.deng@louisville.edu.; Alcohol Research Center, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, USA. zhongbin.deng@louisville.edu.; Hepatobiology & Toxicology Center, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, USA. zhongbin.deng@louisville.edu.
items.abstract: Fungal and bacterial dysbiosis are linked to asthma disease severity, yet how overgrowth of the commensal fungus Candida albicans contributes to disease progression is not fully understood. Here, we show that intestinal aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) deficiency exacerbates house dust mite (HDM)-induced allergic airway disease (AAD) during oral Candida albicans colonization through enhanced IL-17 responsiveness and lung structural cell fucosylation. Intestinal AhR deficiency promotes exaggerated IL-17 responses that promotes neutrophil migration and accumulation in the lung and reshapes the gut microbiota, particularly reducing the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila. Concurrently, increased fucosylation of lung structural cells enhances L-selectin glycan ligand biosynthesis, thereby promoting neutrophil adhesion and retention within inflamed lung tissue. These adherent neutrophils lead to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and tissue injury in epithelial and endothelial compartments. Administration of A. muciniphila or its derived outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), as well as genetic deletion of Fut2, reduces lung fucosylation, suppresses neutrophil adhesion and NET formation, and attenuates Candida albicans-exacerbated AAD. Together, these findings show that intestinal AhR signaling remotely regulates an IL-17- gut microbiota-fucosylation axis that promotes neutrophil adhesion, mitochondrial dysfunction of lung structure cell, and neutrophilic airway inflammation during Candida albicans-associated asthma.

items.title: NYNRIN safeguards leukemia stem cells by sustaining thioredoxin activity to maintain redox homeostasis.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, 400016, China. 103137@cqmu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) primarily rely on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for energy production, a metabolic feature that inevitably generates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS). NYNRIN (NYN domain and retroviral integrase containing) is highly expressed in LSC-like cells and is associated with poor prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Genetic targeting of NYNRIN impairs LSC-like cell maintenance and in vivo leukemogenic capacity in MLL-AF9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-driven AML models, and compromises the in vivo pathogenicity of patient-derived LSC-like cells. Mechanistically, NYNRIN sustains thioredoxin (Trx) activity by functioning as an RNA-binding protein that directly binds and degrades TXNIP mRNA via its NYN domain. Loss of NYNRIN stabilizes TXNIP mRNA, leading to TXNIP accumulation, which disrupts Trx-mediated redox buffering, induces ROS overproduction and mitochondrial dysfunction, and triggers LSC apoptosis. Notably, NYNRIN inhibition potentiates venetoclax efficacy by compromising Trx-mediated ROS clearance, lowering the apoptotic threshold of LSCs. Collectively, our findings reveal a critical NYNRIN-TXNIP-Trx axis that safeguards LSCs by enabling efficient ROS clearance.

items.title: Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Quantum Nanoscience, Kavli Institute of Nanoscience, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. a.f.otte@tudelft.nl.
items.abstract: Atomic nuclear spins are promising candidates in the development of quantum information technologies on a wide variety of physical platforms. Thanks to the high degree of isolation from their environment, nuclear spins show long-lived spin states, but this also poses challenges on their control and readability. Detailed characterization and control over the atomic-scale environment of the nuclear spin become of great importance for their efficient control. In this work, using scanning tunnelling microscopy, we reveal nuclear magnetic resonance on a single on-surface atom. We employ an electron-nuclear double resonance measurement scheme and resolve nuclear spin transitions of a single 47Ti isotope with a nuclear spin of I = 5/2. Our measurements and numerical analysis reveal the nature of hyperfine and quadrupole couplings of the studied system. We also show our ability to address the nuclear spin in the limit of weak hybridization with the electron spin, a requirement for direct control of the nuclear spin in the long-lifetime regime. This investigation of an atomic nuclear spin in a platform with atomic-scale control is a valuable development for other platforms deploying nuclear spins.

items.title: Education-related polygenic scores show different associations with youth mental health in parent-offspring trios.
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Psychology and Language Sciences, University College London, London, UK.; Social, Genetic and Developmental Psychiatry Centre, King's College London, London, UK.
items.abstract: Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children's genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments. We examine whether associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores differ for cognitive and non-cognitive genetic components of educational attainment. These scores aggregate common DNA variants using weights from genome-wide association studies. We analyse 3,223 mother-father-child trios from the UK Millennium Cohort Study using structural equation models that jointly estimate associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores. Here we show that cognitive and non-cognitive education-related polygenic scores are associated with externalising behaviour, including hyperactivity and conduct problems, and internalising behaviour, including anxiety and low mood, across childhood and adolescence. Associations are generally larger in magnitude for externalising than internalising behaviour, with clearer component-specific differences for externalising behaviour. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in education-related polygenic score associations with youth mental health within families.

items.title: Structural dynamics between Argonaute-2 and CK1α promote target RNA release in microRNA-mediated silencing.
items.last_author_affiliation: W. M. Keck Structural Biology Laboratory, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, One Bungtown Road, Cold Spring Harbor, New York, USA. leemor@cshl.edu.; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, One Bungtown Road, Cold Spring Harbor, New York, USA. leemor@cshl.edu.
items.abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins associate with 20-22 nucleotide (nt) long microRNAs (miRNAs) to constitute the functional RISC core and downregulate mRNAs containing complementarity to the seed sequence. Target RNA engagement in RISC stimulates CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of the conserved eukaryotic insertion (EI) in Ago, releasing the target and enabling the RISC complex to suppress additional target sites for efficient miRNA-mediated silencing. Here, we provide a complete structural view of miRNA guide and target binding to human Ago2, showing Ago2 holding the double-stranded guide-target RNA in an untwisted conformation at its center. We visualize the dynamic changes that RISC undergoes as the guide supplementary region progressively base pairs with the target, enabling CK1α binding. Following seed-helix assembly, initial supplementary pairing restricts RISC to a "closed" form, while with half-supplementary pairing, the PAZ domain moves to open RISC to become receptive to CK1α, exhibiting an initial increase in Ago2 phosphorylation. Complete supplementary pairing supports a full PAZ-CK1α interface, allowing for hierarchical phosphorylation of the EI. The combination of target repulsion by EI phosphorylation with an unwound guide-target enables efficient target release to promote RISC turnover.

items.title: A temporal SOX2 engagement cycle at Nanog is linked to molecular crowding and transcriptional states.
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Medical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health, The Charles Perkins Center, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia; The Genome Imaging Centre, Centenary Institute, The University of Sydney, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Missenden Road, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia. Electronic address: mathias.francois@sydney.edu.au.
items.abstract: Stem cell self-renewal relies on transcriptional bursting of pluripotency genes, yet how transcription factors relate temporally to these on and off states remain unclear. We integrate trimodal live-cell imaging of SOX2 mobility, Nanog locus diffusion, and nascent Nanog RNA synthesis with fixed-cell measurements of regulatory factors and RNA to identify temporally distinct SOX2 engagement states associated with putative transcriptional priming and post-elongation in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). At the Nanog locus, we find that SOX2 visiting frequency and dwell time are inversely related to local abundance of regulatory factors and RNA. During productive elongation, high nascent RNA levels coincide with reduced SOX2 repetitive rebinding. After transcript release, lower local RNA and factor abundance are associated with increased SOX2 revisiting, longer residency, and greater locus mobility. These observations support a model in which the temporal SOX2 engagement cycle accompanies transcription-dependent changes in local molecular crowding, providing a dynamic framework for transcriptional priming and post-elongation reset.

items.title: ACAD10 encodes two orphan enzymes in the ether lipid biosynthetic and salvage pathways.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Molecular Biology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Chevy Chase, MD 20815, USA; Harold C. Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA; Hamon Center for Regenerative Science and Medicine, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA. Electronic address: vincent.tagliabracci@utsouthwestern.edu.
items.abstract: Ether lipids play critical roles in membrane dynamics, antioxidant defense, and signaling. They comprise ∼20% of mammalian phospholipids, and disruptions in their metabolism cause severe genetic disorders and are associated with neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases. Ether lipids are synthesized de novo from glycolytic intermediates or salvaged from the diet. While the products of these pathways are known, several key enzymes remain unidentified, including the 1-O-alkylglycerol kinase and the 1-O-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate phosphatase. Here, we show that acyl-CoA dehydrogenase member 10 (ACAD10) catalyzes the phosphorylation of 1-O-alkylglycerols and the dephosphorylation of 1-O-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate. Worms and mice lacking ACAD10 have reduced ether lipid levels and cannot salvage dietary alkylglycerols. Furthermore, individuals from the Akimel O'odham (Pima) tribe carrying ACAD10 polymorphisms show decreased plasma ether lipid levels. Collectively, our findings resolve two long-standing gaps in ether lipid biochemistry and reveal a mechanistic link between ether lipid metabolism and a population-associated risk factor for type 2 diabetes.

items.title: A three-axis structural framework for state-dependent spectral gradients in macaque cortex.
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Systems Science, Beijing Normal University, Beijing 100875, China. Electronic address: yhchen@bnu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Wakefulness and anesthesia are associated with distinct patterns of large-scale brain activity. However, it remains unclear how state-dependent broadband electrophysiological activity corresponds to spectral gradients and the principles underlying cortical structural gradients. Using cortex-wide macaque electrocorticography (ECoG), we identified a dominant cross-frequency spectral gradient that reorganized between wakefulness and anesthesia. We distilled 29 anatomical, molecular, and connectivity maps into three structural categories, from which we derived natural cortical axes of laminar architecture, local microstructure, and afferent wiring range using biologically motivated models. The awake spectral gradient required the joint contribution of all three axes, whereas anesthesia disrupted this balance, reordering spectral-gradient ranks and reducing functional differentiation. Specifically, ketamine anesthesia reduced the long-range afferent contribution of the third axis, whereas supplementary analyses of propofol anesthesia implicated stronger inhibitory control within the local microstructure of the second axis. Together, altered interplay among the three axes may reshape cortical spectral gradients across brain states.

items.title: Fate patterns self-organize through the coupling of structures across cell and supracellular levels of organization.
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Morphogenesis, the Rockefeller University, New York, NY 10065, USA. Electronic address: ashyer@rockefeller.edu.
items.abstract: How patterns of cell state emerge across a tissue field is a fundamental question brought into renewed focus by spatial omics tools that map molecular states onto tissue organization. Here, we investigate how a field of limb progenitor mesenchyme transforms into distinct, adjacent cartilage and soft tissue compartments. We find that mesenchymal tissue fields self-organize their own differentiation through co-constitutive relationships between cell and supracellular structures, which produce cell-extracellular matrix (ECM) or cell-cell-based supracellular cues that canalize cartilage or soft tissue cell fate change, respectively. At the tissue level, bifurcation in intrinsically generated supracellular structures guides the specification of tissue compartment size. We find that Wnt secreted from neighboring epithelial tissue influences mesenchymal cell fate and patterning by functioning as a modulator of cell-supracellular structural coupling. Taken together, our results provide insight into how mesenchymal self-organization interfaces with epithelial signaling to robustly enable a tissue compartmentalization process that initiates the skeleton.

items.title: Autoantibody origins in lupus and upon recurrence post CAR-T therapy.
items.last_author_affiliation: Autoimmunity Laboratory, The Francis Crick Institute, London, UK. Electronic address: carola.vinuesa@crick.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T therapy induces profound remissions in lupus by depleting B cells, challenging the view that disease is sustained by long-lived plasma cells. Using molecular antibody tagging in mouse models of monogenic childhood-onset lupus, we show that autoantibody-producing plasma cells are short-lived and require continuous replenishment from T-bet-dependent precursors derived from long-lived B cell cohorts. The spleen is a major plasma cell reservoir, with perivascular enrichment observed in patients with lupus. Both anti-CD19 and anti-B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR-T therapies eliminate anti-DNA antibodies. Recurrent autoantibodies after anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy derive exclusively from newly generated B cells, whereas those following anti-BCMA CAR-T therapy also arise from treatment-resistant clones. Thus, ongoing B cell-to-plasma cell differentiation, rather than plasma cell longevity, can sustain pathogenic antibody responses in lupus and provides a mechanistic framework for optimizing CAR-T therapies.

items.title: Neural correlates of facial recognition in a social wasp.
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory for Animal Social Evolution and Recognition, Department of Neurobiology and Behavior, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA. Electronic address: msheehan@cornell.edu.
items.abstract: In humans and other primates, faces are special visual objects that are encoded by circuits selective to faces. If specialized circuits are the most efficient way to encode and discriminate among similar-looking objects of high relevance, then we expect that analogous circuits should evolve in other taxa with specialized visual individual recognition abilities. Thus, we surveyed the neural responses to visual objects across the brain of a wasp that has independently evolved specialized facial recognition, Polistes fuscatus. We found a localized population of neurons analogous to face cells, which we term "wasp cells," that selectively fire to front-facing wasp images. Some of these wasp cells encode information about facial patterns, which possibly underlie the unique visual recognition abilities of these wasps. These findings demonstrate high-level feature-selective tuning in an invertebrate and suggest that specialized circuits are an adaptive feature for nervous systems requiring complex visual recognition.

items.title: Transcription factor subtype governs response and resistance to DLL3-directed T cell engagement in small cell lung cancer.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02215, USA. Electronic address: matthew_oser@dfci.harvard.edu.
items.abstract: Although small cell lung cancer (SCLC) comprises transcription factor (TF)-defined molecular subtypes (ASCL1, NEUROD1, and POU2F3), whether these predict therapeutic response or evolve under therapeutic pressure remains unclear. Tarlatamab, a DLL3 × CD3 bispecific T cell engager, has transformed SCLC therapy, yet responses are heterogeneous and resistance develops in most patients. We inferred tumor gene expression from circulating chromatin in patient plasma and developed an immunocompetent syngeneic mouse model to study tarlatamab response and resistance. Across patients and mice, TF subtypes associated with response or resistance. ASCL1 tumors were enriched for response, consistent with DLL3 being an ASCL1 target gene, while NEUROD1 tumors had inferior responses and POU2F3 tumors were intrinsically resistant. Acquired resistance involved selection for a NEUROD1-high state with downregulation of the ASCL1-linked antigen DLL3 or enrichment of regulatory and exhausted T cell programs. These findings support TF-defined subtypes as clinically relevant frameworks for understanding tarlatamab response and resistance in SCLC.

items.title: LPMOcat: an interactive database for comparative structural analysis of lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases
items.abstract: LPMOcat is a comprehensive resource of 161 characterised lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) from all eight CAZy families, in which an automated pipeline integrates data from public databases and, based on a structural alignment, annotates common structural features of LPMOs (e.g. histidine brace, second-sphere residues, loop regions), and calculates per-residue properties (e.g. flexibility, hydrophobicity, hole-hopping pathways). The web application summarises all the gathered information in plots integrated with a similarity tree and allows users to filter the catalogue and compare any set of LPMOs to investigate their structure-function relationships.

items.title: Beyond a single threshold: calibration of CADD v1.7 and AlphaGenome for ACMG/AMP computational evidence across variant classes, model versions, and reference data
items.abstract: Purpose: Computational predictors provide PP3 and BP4 evidence under the ACMG/AMP guidelines, but that evidence holds only within the conditions of its calibration. We asked how far a calibrated threshold travels. Methods: Following a plan fixed before any result, we used the ClinGen local posterior probability method to calibrate CADD v1.7 (Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion) and the AlphaGenome Variant Impact score (AVI) on rare ClinVar missense variants, then changed one condition at a time: variant class, model version, reference set, and gene. Results: Both predictors reached moderate pathogenic and strong benign evidence, and their thresholds held for variants classified after calibration. AVI outperformed CADD in every comparison. Thresholds available in 2024 gave AVI evidence in the final direction for 72.5% of the variants of uncertain significance resolved by 2026, against 60.5% for CADD. Missense thresholds gave false benign evidence to pathogenic noncoding variants. Moving from CADD v1.6 to v1.7 altered the evidence level of a third of variants without improving discrimination, and changing the reference set moved the thresholds. Conclusion: A calibrated threshold belongs to a predictor, a variant class, a model version, and a reference set together. Laboratories should report the source of every threshold they apply.

items.title: FoXSight: Facilitating Computational Hit Identification in Crystallographic Fragment Screening Experiments
items.abstract: X-ray crystallographic fragment screening reveals how small molecules bind to proteins, providing important starting points for drug design. Identifying these weak binding events remains difficult when electron density signals are noisy, partially occupied or obscured by solvent, and campaigns may comprise thousands of datasets. Here, we present FoXSight, a computational method for hit identification in crystallographic compound screening. FoXSight applies Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filtering to multi-reference subtraction maps to detect recurring, target-specific density features associated with bound ligands. Its output maps remain visually interpretable and support subsequent ligand modeling. We evaluated FoXSight on in-house and public datasets spanning seven protein targets, comparing its maps with PanDDA where suitable comparison data were available. FoXSight was successfully used as the primary hit identification tool in a challenging crystallographic fragment screening campaign for human Cathepsin L, where the output of established methods was impractical to inspect systematically.

items.title: CA19-9-associated transcriptional programs in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma are linked to survival and drug sensitivity
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer contains diverse cancer-cell states that complicate treatment selection. We asked whether targeted transcriptomics of glycan-defined PDAC cells would reveal novel and clinically informative subtypes. Spatial profiling of CA19-9-positive regions from 3 tumors with divergent clinical outcomes identified four transcriptional programs: inflammation and tissue remodeling (Cluster 1), proliferation (Cluster 2), antigen presentation and differentiation (Cluster 3), and protein synthesis (Cluster 4). These programs were recovered across 108 Visium sections from 39 patients, 161 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas, and 37 cell lines with drug-response data. Among 31 tumors with broadly elevated program expression, eight Cluster 1 dominant tumors had poorer survival than the remaining 23. Exploratory drug-response analyses identified cluster-associated sensitivity and resistance patterns, including greater moexipril sensitivity with higher Cluster 1 activity. These findings demonstrate targeted profiling of glycan-defined PDAC populations to uncover cancer-cell-intrinsic therapeutic vulnerabilities, and they reveal CA19-9-associated molecular diversity with program-specific therapeutic candidates.

items.title: Diversity of Environmental and Genome-Associated Eukaryotic Circular Rep-Encoding Single-Stranded DNA Viruses
items.corresponding_institution: University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa
items.abstract: Circular Rep-encoding single-stranded (CRESS) DNA viruses are widespread across diverse environments, yet their genomic diversity, evolutionary relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses by integrating replication-associated protein (Rep) sequences from environmental viral metagenomes, publicly available viral references, and endogenous viral elements (EVEs) identified in fungal and algal genomes. Genome-wide screening revealed numerous EVEs distributed across diverse fungal and algal lineages, highlighting the potential historical associations between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic hosts. Phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among CRESS DNA viruses, including sequences that could not be assigned to currently recognized viral families. Yet, several of these unclassified sequences formed well-supported monophyletic clades, suggesting that existing taxonomic classifications may require further revision. Furthermore, phylogenetic relationships within and among established viral families suggest that existing taxonomic boundaries may not fully capture the evolutionary diversity of these viruses. The phylogenetic placement of fungal and algal EVEs alongside environmental and reference viral sequences further provides insights into the evolutionary relationships between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic genomes. Collectively, our findings expand the known evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses, identify distinct viral lineages requiring further taxonomic evaluation, and provide a framework for investigating their genomic evolution, taxonomic relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts.

items.title: Pharmacogenomic diversity at tuberculosis-treatment loci across African populations: phased haplotypes, regulatory architecture and NAT2 acetylator inference
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Microbiology and Parasitology, St. Francis University College of Health and Allied Sciences (SFUCHAS), Ifakara, Tanzania; Tanzania Infectious Dise
items.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis imposes a major public-health burden in Africa, while variation in isoniazid and rifampicin disposition creates opportunities for improved pharmacotherapy. The population architecture of extended, phased pharmacogenomic backgrounds remains less well characterized than individual marker frequencies. Methods: We analyzed high-coverage, phased GRCh38 genomes from 661 unrelated individuals sampled from five continental-African and two African-diaspora populations at NAT2, SLCO1B1, CES2, HLA-B, NR1I2 and UGT1A1. We integrated frequency differentiation, reduced phased signatures, linkage disequilibrium, functional annotation and NAT2 core-allele inference with individual-clustered permutation tests. Results: The six loci contributed 17,223 annotated variant records and 276 entries in a capped frequency-differentiation register. Exact NAT2 core-definition matching was achieved for 1,321/1,322 chromosomes (99.92%), and determinate genotype-inferred acetylator categories for 620/661 individuals (93.80%). Among the sampled continental-African populations, 35-site noncore background distributions differed within NAT2 *5 (BH-adjusted q=0.000100), *4 (q=0.024733) and *6 (q=0.000350) groups. Distinct phased and linkage architectures also characterized transporter, hydrolysis, regulatory and HLA-B genomic regions. Conclusion: African population-associated variation extends beyond commonly used pharmacogenetic allele definitions. The observed NAT2 backgrounds and complementary locus signatures provide a foundation for targeted molecular studies and prospective pharmacokinetic validation that could inform future population-responsive TB treatment research.

items.title: Divergent immune trajectories distinguish resistance and susceptibility to bacterial leaf streak in wheat
items.abstract: Bacterial leaf streak (BLS) is an increasingly important disease affecting several cereal crops. The mechanisms linking quantitative trait loci for resistance to downstream immune response against BLS in wheat remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a chromosome-scale genome assembly of the BLS resistant cultivar Boost. With de novo annotation of Boost and Timstein (susceptible cultivar) assemblies, we established a cultivar-resolved framework for dissecting BLS resistance. Both cultivars encoded highly similar immune receptor repertoires, but the major resistance locus, QBls.fcu-3B.1, comprised a divergent receptor kinase haplotype with extensive structural variations, divergent tandem receptor arrays, and constitutively elevated expression of multiple receptor kinases in the resistant cultivar. Candidate receptor kinases in Boost exhibited conserved intracellular kinase domains but substantial divergence among extracellular recognition domains relative to their syntenic homologs in Timstein. Dual reference transcriptome analyses at 24, 48, and 96 hours after inoculation (HAI) revealing contrasting immune trajectories in resistant and susceptible cultivars. Boost progressed through a focused signaling transition at 48 HAI, followed by coordinated activation of several defense modules, such as antimicrobial metabolism, cell wall reinforcement, transcriptional regulation, and immune homeostasis. In contrast, the susceptible cultivar underwent coordinated repression of these defense-related modules together with chromatin-associated transcriptional changes and induction of host transcriptional machinery during disease establishment. Our findings suggest that quantitative resistance to BLS is associated not simply with immune receptor composition, but also with constitutive immune surveillance and temporal coordination of downstream defense, providing a putative mechanistic framework linking natural genomic variations to quantitative BLS resistance in wheat.

items.title: FiberTron enables regulatory variant effect prediction and testing from multi-omic long reads of a single sample
items.abstract: State-of-the-art sequence-to-function models are trained on large compendia of public data to predict regulatory activity across hundreds of cell types. However, they are not designed to interpret individual genomes, effects in under-sampled cell types, or provide a comprehensive view of how genetic variation influences complex diseases. Here we show that a single sample profiled with Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq contains enough information to train such a model from scratch. FiberTron, a 12M parameter convolutional-transformer model, takes 524 kb of reference sequence and predicts CpG methylation, chromatin accessibility and strand-specific transcript coverage at base-pair resolution (median Pearson's r of 0.85-0.97 on held-out chromosomes). Trained in under a day on a single four-GPU node, our HG002 model performs on par with models such as AlphaGenome on dsQTL and eQTL variant effect prediction tasks, despite being over an order of magnitude smaller. As training uses reference sequence only, each sample's phased multi-omic long reads remain available to test its variant-effect predictions. FiberTron recapitulates OAS1 splicing variation associated with COVID-19 risk, recovers 79% of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, identifies oncogenic TERT promoter and TAL1 enhancer mutations, and predicts EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript expression and its unique chromatin imprint in a rare clear cell sarcoma patient sample. Lightweight single-sample training brings base-resolution interpretation of non-coding variation within reach of individual laboratories.

items.title: A Two-Stage YOLO-Swin Transformer Pipeline for Cross-Dataset White Blood Cell Classification
items.abstract: Background: White blood cell (WBC) classification across datasets is challenged by differences in staining, image context, and class distributions. Methods: We developed a two-stage YOLO11-Swin Transformer pipeline. In the first stage, WBC detection and context-preserving cropping, a YOLO11 detector finds the leukocyte in each uncropped image and produces a cell-focused crop that retains the surrounding background. In the second stage, WBC classification, a Swin Transformer (Swin-B) assigns the crop to one of nine cell types. The classifier was trained on detector-cropped cells from five public datasets, so the first stage supplies the same kind of input at test time; morphology-preserving color augmentation addressed staining variation, and class-weighted cross-entropy addressed class imbalance. WBCBench2026, a public benchmark not used for training, served for external evaluation in seven harmonized classes, scored by macro-F1 (the mean of per-class F1). Further analyses removed the first stage or masked the background, compared classifier backbones, held out each training dataset (leave-one-dataset-out, LODO), and tested a second split (Phase-2) with about 60% synthetically degraded images. Results: The full pipeline reached an external macro-F1 of 0.879{+/-}0.006 on 8,080 benchmark images. With uncropped images as input, the same crop-trained classifier reached 0.627{+/-}0.039, and crops that kept the surrounding background outperformed background-masked crops (0.867 versus 0.760). With identical detector-cropped input, Swin-B outperformed convolutional baselines (0.863 versus 0.718-0.813), and its advantage over ResNet50 persisted across three training configurations. In LODO, macro-F1 on the held-out dataset ranged from 0.59 to 0.91, revealing source-specific variation not fully covered by the remaining datasets. On Phase-2, macro-F1 was 0.769{+/-}0.002. Two hematologists independently reviewed all 205 blast- or promyelocyte-related model-benchmark disagreements and gave the same verdict on 73 crops (35.6%): 21 model right, 43 model wrong, 9 ambiguous. Conclusions: The proposed two-stage pipeline achieved strong cross-dataset WBC classification performance. Context-preserving cropping was essential for the crop-trained classifier, and the LODO findings support representing the same classes across diverse sources when developing robust WBC classifiers.

items.title: WildTrust-UAV: uncertainty-aware wildlife detection with privacy-preserving spatial disclosure and verifiable inference provenance
items.corresponding_institution: Pennsylvania State University College of Information Sciences and Technology
items.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery has made wildlife surveys faster and safer, but a detected animal is not yet a conservation record. Detector confidence scores are often poorly calibrated, exact coordinates of threatened species can expose them to harm, and an observation is rarely tied back to the image, model, and settings that produced it. WildTrust-UAV addresses these three problems in one framework. It pairs a YOLO11 detector with stochastic-view uncertainty estimation, temperature scaling fitted on validation data, a selective gateway that accepts, defers, or rejects each detection, role-based disclosure of animal locations, and a provenance record that hashes the source image, model, configuration, prediction, uncertainty, timestamp, and nonce. Records are aggregated in a Merkle tree and signed with Ed25519 so that any observation can be verified independently. We report three evaluations on the public WAID dataset. In the detection experiment, two YOLO11n runs reached mAP@0.50 of 0.901 and 0.903 and mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.527 on a 2,000-image held-out test set. In a separate reliability experiment on 122,720 test detections, temperature scaling reduced expected calibration error from 0.0715 to 0.0179 and the Brier score from 0.0353 to 0.0222. Composite uncertainty identified erroneous detections with an AUROC of 0.904, although confidence alone did better (0.992). Deferring the least reliable detections lowered selective risk from 0.722 at near-full coverage to 0.610 at 69.9% coverage, so considerable error remains in the candidate set. In the provenance experiment, the verifier rejected all 4,500 tampered submissions across nine attack scenarios and accepted all 500 genuine controls, with batch construction and signing taking 0.1 to 2.5 ms. Location policies used synthetic coordinates, and the ledger is a local prototype. Calibration and verifiable records can thus be added to a UAV detection pipeline at low cost, while combining uncertainty signals does not automatically improve error detection.

items.title: CheekAI: An explainable, deep learning epigenetic aging clock based on lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies
items.abstract: The human methylome is poorly understood and, as such, the vast majority of epigenetic aging clocks are unexplainable black boxes. To address this, we created CheekAI, a robust deep learning model that uses lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies (EBPs) to predict age. Trained using a longitudinal dataset of 25,400 adult buccal DNA methylation samples derived from 14,716 distinct adults, we used principal components and multi-objective optimization to produce a clock that is explainable, reproducible, responsive, and accurate. The Pearson correlation with chronological age is 0.969, the mean absolute error is 2.49 years, and the intraclass correlation coefficient across 679 replicate pairs is 0.990. CheekAI was significantly associated with a plethora of lifestyle and health variables, including resting heart rate, omega-3 intake, ultra-processed food intake, daily step count, resistance training, and time spent in nature. When applied to external saliva and buccal datasets, CheekAI significantly captured a variety of signals, including smoking and oesophageal cancer. CheekAI was also significantly reduced by a multifactorial lifestyle intervention and this reduction was driven by improvements in dietary and metabolic EBPs. This novel artificial intelligence model represents the first instance of a buccal epigenetic aging clock that utilizes EBPs to offer interpretability and actionability.

items.title: Local wavefront alignment with corrected free-end penalty
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Comparative Biomedicine, Key Laboratory of Systems Biomedicine (MOE), Institute of Systems Biomedicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong university
items.abstract: Background: Pairwise alignment of nucleotide and protein sequences is a fundamental problem in bioinformatics. Wavefront alignment (WFA) is a groundbreaking algorithmic advance that reduces the time complexity of exact (semi-)global pairwise alignment with affine gap penalties from O(N2) to O(sN). Despite its success, WFA has yet to be extended to the local sequence alignment scope. Results: In this work, we propose a local wavefront alignment (lWFA) which generalizes WFA to the local alignment scope and preserves both the O(sN) time and the O(sN) to O(s2) space complexity. We also propose the bidirectional lWFA (lBiWFA), which reduces the space complexity of lWFA from O(s2) to O(s) while maintaining the time complexity as O(sN). Benchmarks show that lWFA and lBiWFA outperform current exact local alignment libraries like SeqAn and Parasail in aligning long sequences with error rate less than 5%. Conclusions: We suggest to use lBiWFA over lWFA because it has negligible memory footprint for aligning reads up to 20kbp, and is faster than lWFA except for short reads with very low error rates. According to the real-data benchmarks, lBiWFA are faster than SeqAn and Parasail for aligning NGS short reads with 0.1%[~]1% error rate and ONT long reads with 3%[~]5% error rate. However, for reads sequenced by legacy long-read platforms with 10%[~]15% error rate, SeqAn and Parasail are faster. Nevertheless, lBiWFA has a competitive speed for reads with error rate up to 10%. One may choose lBiWFA over SeqAn and Parasail if the memory usage is the major concern.

items.title: BiocPy: A Framework for Cross-Platform Genomic Data andMethods Interoperability
items.abstract: Bioconductor provides standardized data structures and statistical methods for high-throughput genomic analysis in R, whereas Python has become a primary environment for machine learning, image analysis, and general-purpose data science. Combining tools across both ecosystems often requires ad-hoc file conversions or embedded language runtimes that can lose metadata, introduce maintenance overhead, or lead to subtle differences in downstream results. Here, we present BiocPy, a collection of Python packages that support cross-language genomic workflows through three complementary layers: (1) native Python implementations of Bioconductor's core data structures; (2) lossless data exchange via direct reading and writing of serialized R (.rds) objects and the language-neutral ArtifactDB format for persistent, multi-stage pipelines; and (3) a cross-platform method development paradigm built on shared C++ libraries wrapped across R, Python, and WebAssembly to support identical statistical analyses across environments. All packages in the BiocPy ecosystem are published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) with source code hosted at [https://github.com/BiocPy].

items.title: An AI agent guides a pipeline for selective protein interaction inhibitors from discovery across targets to preclinical evaluation
items.abstract: A protein can engage multiple partners, making it challenging to disrupt disease-associated interactions while preserving others. We developed Bivexia, an AI agent that guides a multistage pipeline from discovery and de novo design through preclinical evaluation. Its decision rules are fixed in advance, and each prospective selection by the agent is cryptographically committed before testing. The objective is to discover small molecules that disrupt specified interactions of a target protein while preserving others. A compound advanced by Bivexia bound LAG-3 with nanomolar affinity and disrupted its interactions with tau and amyloid-{beta} while preserving binding to MHC class II and FGL1. It reduced tau and amyloid-{beta} burden in independent cohorts across two mouse models. The same rules gave three of nine hits on PrP and two of nine on LRP1, none in random controls. Our findings establish a framework for AI agents to pursue defined interaction selectivity across targets.

items.title: Convergence of Independently Established Oncogenes in a Combined Breast and Ovarian Cancer Model: Hub Gene Validation and identification of potential Food-Derived therapeutics.
items.abstract: Breast and ovarian cancers share molecular alterations that may reveal common therapeutic targets. Here, we integrated six Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets to identify shared transcriptional changes across the two cancers. Independent differential expression analysis followed by direction-specific intersection identified 396 shared differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 192 upregulated and 204 downregulated genes. Protein-protein interaction analysis prioritized ten hub genes: AURKA, AURKB, BCL2, BIRC5, CCNA2, CDK1, FOXO1, KIF11, PTEN, and TOP2A. Functional enrichment highlighted cell-cycle regulation, mitotic spindle organization, and p53-associated signalling. Independent expression assessment using GEPIA2 identified seven hub genes significantly upregulated in both cancers, while FOXO1 was downregulated. Regulatory network analysis further identified candidate transcription factors and miRNAs potentially associated with these hubs. For therapeutic exploration, a 70,478-compound FooDB library was progressively filtered to 233 candidates using physicochemical, structural-alert, machine-learning-based bioactivity, and ADMET criteria. Molecular docking against eight selected druggable hubs, followed by decoy benchmarking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations, prioritized three complexes: CDK1-artonin L, AURKB-taraxacin, and KIF11-L-thyronine. CDK1-artonin L demonstrated the strongest overall computational support, whereas the AURKB and KIF11 complexes showed differing levels of binding and energetic evidence. This study provides an integrated multi-cohort framework for identifying shared molecular hubs in breast and ovarian cancer and prioritizing food-derived compounds for further investigation. The findings nominate CDK1, AURKB, and KIF11 for experimental evaluation.

items.title: GlycanPUG: WURCS-Based Heterogeneous Graph Pretraining for Structurally Ambiguous Glycans
items.corresponding_institution: East China University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Background: Glycans orchestrate diverse biological processes, yet they remain underrepresented in computational biology compared to proteins and nucleic acids. Although WURCS 2.0 provides a machine-readable structural representation that preserves uncertainty, the evaluated IUPAC-based deterministic workflow processes 43.1% of the GlyCosmos-derived cohort examined here, motivating approaches that retain structural ambiguity. Methods: To overcome this limitation, GlycanPUG (Probabilistic Uncertainty-aware Graph) was introduced as a pretrained graph model for glycan representation learning. By leveraging WURCS 2.0, GlycanPUG represents candidate linkages and substituent attachments using weighted edges and uncertainty attributes within a heterogeneous graph framework. A 4-layer Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with a dedicated node pre-enhancement module aggregates edge features weighted by the assigned edge weights, enabling representation of supported structurally ambiguous glycans without selecting a single resolved structure. The model is pretrained on a preprocessed subset of the GlyTouCan1 repository, which contained 253,596 entries before filtering. After excluding entries linked to downstream tasks and applying sequential structural filtering, 167,020 samples remained and were used for pretraining. Pretraining comprised nine self-supervised tasks. Results: Benchmarking on the GlycanML dataset demonstrates that GlycanPUG shows competitive performance relative to GlycanGT across multi-label taxonomy classification and binary immunogenicity prediction. Crucially, on datasets natively containing structural uncertainties (GlyCosmos, GlyConnect), GlycanPUG effectively processes additional structurally ambiguous entries, achieving 83.5% processable coverage across all glycans from all biological sources in GlyCosmos, with taxonomic classification performance (e.g., mean macro F1 of 0.7376 for Domain). Ablation of the node pre-enhancement module reduces macro F1, and post-hoc analysis identifies rank-dependent associations between structural uncertainty and prediction errors. All results reported above are averaged over ten independent random seeds (1-10). Conclusions: GlycanPUG broadens the set of glycans that can be represented while retaining supported structural ambiguities.

items.title: Structural clustering of paired αβ T-cell receptor repertoires recovers antigen-specific convergence beyond sequence similarity
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Chemistry and Nuffield Department of Medicine, University of Oxford
items.abstract: T-cell receptor (TCR) antigen recognition depends on the three-dimensional geometry of the paired {beta} complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), which primary sequence does not fully capture. Most repertoire-clustering methods group receptors by CDR3 motifs, sequence distance or V-J gene usage, and may miss receptors that differ in sequence but adopt similar loop conformations. We present SPACE-TCR (Structural Profiling of Alpha-Beta Clonotypes by Epitope), which stratifies predicted paired {beta} backbone models by CDR length, aligns them on conserved framework anchors and clusters them by C RMSD across the CDRs. On an independently curated benchmark of 4,779 paired CD8 TCRs spanning 367 epitopes, 94.6% of SPACE-TCR clusters at the focal 0.75 [A] threshold had purity [≥] 0.9, close to ClusTCR (97.3%), while clustering more than twice as many unique CDR3{beta} (10.4% versus 4.7%); every method that clustered more did so at markedly lower purity. SPACE-TCR had the lowest polyspecificity (5.4%), and 22.7% of its high-purity clusters were sequence-diverse or sequence-unrelated, categories rarely recovered by the evaluated CDR3{beta}-similarity methods. With increasing unannotated repertoire background, it kept higher purity than the evaluated sequence-based methods across all available comparisons (30.4% at 89.2% noise, compared with 15.0% for TCRMatch). Paired structural clustering therefore complements sequence-based analysis, recovering convergent receptor families that sequence criteria miss.

items.title: Confidence-guided spatial gene expression inference for reliability-aware prognostic analysis from histology
items.abstract: Inferring spatial gene expression from histology images offers a promising strategy for extending spatial molecular profiling to large-scale clinical tissue archives. However, existing approaches face two major challenges: limited generalizability of single-cell expression inference across datasets and platforms, and the lack of reliable estimates of prediction uncertainty, which compromise downstream biological and clinical analyses. Here, we present REGAIN, a framework for spatial gene expression inference at both single-cell and spot resolutions with prediction confidence. Across tissue sections, independent datasets and platforms, REGAIN improved spatial gene expression prediction and downstream analysis. Confidence-guided selection further enriched for cells with more accurately recovered expression profiles and improved cell-type annotation, while confidence-weighted clustering enhanced spatial-domain identification. Beyond assessing prediction quality, confidence mapping reveals greater heterogeneity in gene expression predictability across spatial domains than across broad cell types, with differences persisting within the same cell type and associated with tumor progression-related cell states and local microenvironmental context. Importantly, in 766 patients from the TCGA-BRCA cohort, confidence weighting enhanced the prognostic value of histology-inferred spatial molecular features, yielding stronger prognostic associations and identifying additional prognostic information beyond age and PAM50 molecular subtype. These confidence-weighted features also showed improved prognostic discrimination compared with clinical variables alone or combined with unweighted spatial molecular features. Together, REGAIN marks a shift in histology-based spatial gene expression inference from a focus on predictive accuracy toward a reliability-aware paradigm, demonstrating that prediction confidence provides biological insights into morphology-expression coupling and enhances the clinical informativeness of inferred spatial molecular features.

items.title: Evaluating the Nanopore Inosine Model for ADAR-Dependent A-to-I RNA Editing Detection
items.abstract: Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (dRNA-seq) reads native RNA molecules, and its basecaller now includes models that detect RNA modifications directly, among them inosine, the product of adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes. These models are increasingly used, but how reliably they detect modifications in biological samples has rarely been tested. We evaluated the Dorado inosine model in a mouse macrophage cell line, comparing wild-type cells with ADAR1-knockout cells and in vitro transcribed RNA, before and after an inflammatory stimulus that increases editing. As a reference, we used the editing sites identified by Illumina sequencing of the same cells. We assessed whether the model distinguishes edited from unedited RNA, which negative control is needed to identify editing sites, how many reference sites are recovered, and why sites are missed. The confidence of the Nanopore inosine model alone was not sufficient to identify editing, and a matched ADAR-deficient control was essential. Even with this control, detection was limited by sequencing depth, by low editing levels and by basecalling errors at edited positions. Nanopore sequencing can detect A-to-I editing, but its inosine calls require an ADAR-deficient control and sufficient depth, and should be confirmed by an orthogonal method.

items.title: To sort or to hash? Revisiting k-mer counting
items.abstract: Motivation: Counting k-mers in large genomic datasets is a foundational primitive in bioinformatics, supporting applications such as genome assembly, variant discovery, metagenomic profiling, and sequence database indexing. As sequencing throughput grows, k-mer counting is routinely applied to collections of hundreds to thousands of files. Even a modest per-file speedup compounds into hours of saved computation across such collections. Methods: Sorting and hashing are the two main ways of counting k-mers, and practice has largely settled on the former, of which KMC3 (Kokot et al., 2017) is the most refined expression. We reconsider this choice and analyze both approaches using a cost model that charges computation and memory transfers together. We show that the outcome of the comparison rests on two matters: how abundant the k-mers are, and whether the hash tables fit in cache. Sorting is faster only when data is mostly unique and the hash tables do not fit in cache. We then design a k-mer counting algorithm in the light of this analysis. We adopt the consolidated paradigm based on first partitioning the k-mers by their minimizer, thus obtaining partitions of super-k-mers, and then counting each partition independently in parallel. In particular, super-k-mers are deduplicated before counting, and the number of partitions is chosen so that the hash tables fit in cache whenever possible. The algorithm avoids writing temporary data to disk if enough internal memory is available. Results: We implemented this strategy in a tool named Tuna and show that it is faster than KMC3 on all but one of our inputs, spanning bacterial and human assemblies, metagenomes and read sets, by up to 4.3x. The advantage of Tuna compared to KMC3 in the counting step alone widens to 6.8x as k-mer abundance grows, as the analysis predicts. On the largest input tested, 614 GB of human sequencing reads, Tuna counts within 4 GB of memory and 0.7 TB of temporary disk. On that input the two tools finish within 1.1x of each other under the full 256 GB budget, and restricting every tool to the same 8 GB budget widens the advantage of Tuna over KMC3 to 1.8x. Software: The software is freely available at github.com/vicLeva/tuna under the MIT license.

items.title: Disentangling within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
items.corresponding_institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Recent advances in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics have enabled high-resolution characterization of gene expression and cellular organization in situ. Resolving within-cell-type heterogeneity is essential for understanding how cellular states relate to tissue function and disease. However, imperfect cell segmentation and RNA spillover can contaminate cell-level expression profiles, obscuring intrinsic expression patterns and generating spurious variation. Existing decontamination methods can struggle to distinguish intrinsic variation from contamination when both are inferred from spatial measurements alone, and may suppress genuine state-associated signals when within-cell-type heterogeneity is not explicitly modeled. Here we present Dancer, a reference-guided probabilistic framework that disentangles within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination by combining cell-type-specific gene programs learned from single-cell data with explicit modeling of intrinsic expression, neighboring-cell contamination and background RNA. Across multiple human tumor datasets with varying gene compositions and panel sizes, Dancer improves cell-type separation and expression specificity while preserving identity-associated signals, achieving superior overall performance in benchmark comparisons. Inferred gene program activities reveal within-cell-type heterogeneity in the form of distinct cellular states and continuous spatial gradients associated with local tissue environments, while reference-guided panel expansion extends molecular characterization beyond the measured genes. Together, Dancer supports accurate transcript decontamination and more faithful interpretation of cellular heterogeneity within its native tissue context.

items.title: Multi-omics causal deep learning reveals regulatory structure while interventions refine perturbation predictions
items.abstract: Inferring gene regulation from single-cell data is difficult because observational measurements cannot distinguish correlation from causation and access to perturbational data, especially with multiple modalities, remains limited. Here we present the Cross-Modal Causal Variational Autoencoder (CMC-VAE), which learns a network linking genes and proteins (gene-gene, protein-protein and gene-protein) in the latent space and maps each connection back onto measured features. Trained on 809,130 observational CITE-seq profiles, CMC-VAE recovers co-expression, transcription factor regulons and immune signalling programs, and learns a sparse cross-modal map enriched for transcript-protein cognate pairs. On three CRISPR screens used during development, it ranks knockout-responsive genes better than correlation and latent-VAE baselines. Fitted to a screen's unperturbed control cells, without perturbation labels, the model translates measured knockout RNA responses into protein responses better than a correlation map and cognate transcripts. The direction of gene-to-gene regulation, however, is not recovered from observational data. On the CITE-seq screens, fine-tuning only the latent network improves held-out response correlation, mainly by learning a response shared across knockouts. On larger Perturb-seq screens, with about 1,000 training perturbations, fine-tuning the latent network learns gene-specific effects that transfer to held-out genes, more so than a gene-level causal model fine-tuned on the same cells, and in simulation, such interventions also restore edge orientations that observational training leaves unresolved.

items.title: PathwayTheme: identifying and attributing pathway-level axes of variation in omics data
items.abstract: Exploring gene expression datasets often involves delineating principal axes of variation corresponding to either biological or technical variables. Principal component analysis (PCA) is typically employed as it uses all genes, reflecting global relationships between samples. Existing tools decompose gene expression first and interpret components afterwards. However, gene-level components are sensitive to sparsity and difficult to relate directly to biology, signals carried by low-variance components are easily overlooked, and differential pathway analysis is usually performed separately, on thresholded gene lists. PathwayTheme addresses these limitations by reversing the order of operations: per-sample pathway scores are generated first and then decomposed by PCA, so that each component is defined by pathways and can be tested directly against biological and technical variables. PathwayTheme further incorporates a statistical framework for supervised differential pathway enrichment that does not require thresholded gene lists, with Gene Ontology results summarised into themes. Applied to a published paediatric cancer cohort, PathwayTheme separated technical from biological axes and identified components distinguishing sample types, diagnoses and genetic subgroups, including rare groups represented by low-variance components.

items.title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
items.corresponding_institution: Information Hub, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); AI for Science Center, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; School of E
items.abstract: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. Together, UltraMS and UltraAtlas constitute a generalizable framework for structural elucidation and biological discovery from tandem mass spectra, empowering the comprehensive exploration of the largely undeciphered metabolomes across different domains of life.

items.title: Measuring Cell Type Resolved Aging Through Long-Read Sequencing
items.corresponding_institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School
items.abstract: Epigenetic clocks based on bulk blood DNA methylation are powerful tools for quantifying biological aging, but bulk measurements conflate cell-autonomous epigenetic changes with age-related shifts in blood cell composition. Here, we develop LongReadClock, a set of cell-type-resolved epigenetic aging clocks constructed from cohort-scale long-read whole-genome sequencing of bulk blood without physical cell sorting. Individual sequencing reads were classified using seven target-specific blood-cell models using methylation-based log-likelihood-ratio scoring against a purified-cell atlas. LongReadClock achieved mean absolute errors of 2.8-5.7 years on held-out samples across bulk blood and digitally resolved cell types. Covariate-adjusted analyses identified associations that differed across cell types, including lower mean epigenetic age deviation (EAD) in males in B-cell and NK-cells, associations of systolic blood pressure and resting heart rate with myeloid EAD, and higher NK-cell EAD in participants with asthma. A Fisher-information screen was used to prioritize age-informative genomic windows and to explore read-level methylation patterns at the ELOVL2 locus. These results support cell-type-resolved epigenetic age inference from cohort-scale long-read methylation data from standard bulk blood samples.

items.title: CIP2A is a biomarker for progression and poor prognosis in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
items.abstract: The incidence of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is rising worldwide, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic options for recurrent and metastatic disease. Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a keyt tumor suppressor, and its inhibition promotes malignant progression. Here, we investigated the role of the cancerous inhibitor of PP2A (CIP2A) in cSCC progression. RNA-sequencing, oligonucleotide array-based expression, and qRT-PCR analysis demonstrated elevated CIP2A mRNA levels in cSCC cells compared with normal human epidermal keratinocytes (NHEKs). Western blotting confirmed higher CIP2A protein production in cSCC cells than in NHEKs. Analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing data from cSCC showed CIP2A expression in epithelial cells and fibroblasts. Silencing CIP2A with specific siRNAs reduced cSCC cell growth and viability by inhibiting MEK1 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation. In vivo, strong CIP2A immunostaining was observed in tumor cells of primary cSCCs and cSCC metastases, whereas staining was absent or weak in all actinic keratoses and most cSCC in situ samples. Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed that patients with high CIP2A expression had significantly worse disease-specific survival than those with low expression. These findings identify CIP2A as a clinically relevant oncogene in cSCC progression, with elevated expression in invasive primary tumors and metastases. CIP2A may serve as a biomarker of cSCC progression and metastasis, as well as a potential therapeutic target in advanced and metastatic cSCC.

items.title: A hidden mitotic vulnerability emerges from BCAT1 redox-motif disruption in Ewing sarcoma
items.abstract: Cancer cells must keep oxidative stress and chromosome-segregation errors within tolerable limits to sustain rapid proliferation. Because redox homeostasis supports faithful chromosome segregation, disrupting redox-dependent mitotic safeguards could drive chromosomal instability (CIN) beyond cell tolerance and suppress tumor growth. Here, we investigated whether selectively disrupting redox-dependent safeguards could uncouple oxidative-stress adaptation from faithful chromosome segregation, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability at the interface of metabolic regulation and genome maintenance. We used Ewing sarcoma (EwS) as a model because it combines low genomic complexity with elevated oxidative stress and limited redox-buffering capacity. A survival analysis of cell-cycle-associated genes prioritized branched-chain amino acid transaminase 1 (BCAT1), whose high expression was associated with adverse outcomes in both primary and relapsed EwS. Functional genomics analyses revealed that BCAT1 is transcriptionally regulated by the EwS-specific EWSR1::FLI1 fusion oncoprotein through a distal enhancer-like GGAA microsatellite. Using prime-edited endogenous alleles and isogenic cell models, we found that disrupting BCAT1 redox-active CXXC motif increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and impaired recovery from it. Motif disruption also caused chromosome-segregation defects and DNA damage, reduced three-dimensional growth, and suppressed tumor formation and metastasis in vivo. By contrast, catalytic inactivation had limited effects. Although acute BCAT1 protein depletion reduced proliferation and tumor formation, constitutive BCAT1 knockout cells remained viable in culture and reduced tumor formation less than motif disruption. Mechanistically, CXXC motif disruption reduced casein kinase 2 (CK2) activity and increased Aurora kinase B (AURKB) activity, whereas BCAT1 degradation left CK2 activity unchanged and reduced AURKB activity. The enhanced sensitivity of CXXC-mutant cells to AURKB inhibition suggests a therapeutic vulnerability that could be exploited in BCAT1-wild-type EwS cells through combined CK2 and AURKB inhibition with silmitasertib and barasertib, increasing maximal growth inhibition and lowering the barasertib concentration required to suppress proliferation. Collectively, these findings reveal a mitotic vulnerability associated with BCAT1 redox-motif disruption that is not fully reproduced by protein loss and can be therapeutically exploited using clinically evaluated CK2 and AURKB inhibitors.

items.title: Androgen Receptor and ACSL4 Interplay as Therapeutic Targets in Breast Cancer
items.corresponding_institution: Universidad de Buenos Aires, Facultad de Medicina; CONICET - Universidad de Buenos Aires, INBIOMED
items.abstract: High Acyl-CoA synthetase 4 (ACSL4) expression is implicated in the development and progression of aggressive tumors, poor prognosis, and unfavorable clinical outcomes, as observed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). The androgen receptor (AR) has emerged as a therapeutic target in AR-positive TNBCs, while treatment options are even more limited for quadruple-negative breast cancer (QNBC), the AR-negative TNBC subtype. This study investigates the reciprocal regulation between AR and ACSL4 and evaluates their potential as therapeutic targets in breast cancer. Analysis of patient datasets and expression profiling in human breast cancer cells revealed an inverse correlation between ACSL4 and AR expression. We show that ectopic AR expression decreases ACSL4 promoter activity, mRNA, and protein levels, whereas AR inhibition increases ACSL4 expression in breast cancer cells. We demonstrate that AR acts as a repressor by binding to an androgen response element on the ACSL4 promoter. Moreover, ectopic ACSL4 expression decreased AR levels, while pharmacological ACSL4 inhibition or silencing increased AR expression, supporting a negative regulatory loop. To investigate whether ACSL4 inhibition sensitizes QNBC cells to antiandrogen treatment, PRGL493 and bicalutamide (ACSL4 and AR inhibitors, respectively) were combined, producing synergistic inhibitory effects on cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. This combination also showed strong suppressive effects in cancer cell extravasation, a key step in the process of cancer metastasis, using a zebrafish xenotransplantation model. These findings show that ACSL4 inhibition sensitizes QNBC cells to antiandrogen therapy due to reciprocal negative regulation between ACSL4 and AR, providing a novel promising strategy for aggressive breast cancer subtypes.

items.title: Glycogen fuels and spatially regulates nucleotide biosynthesis in cancer
items.abstract: Cancer cells must coordinate metabolic substrate availability with the organization of biosynthetic pathways to sustain proliferation. Glycogen accumulates in many cancers, but its function extends beyond glucose storage. Here, we show that glycogen regulates nucleotide biosynthesis through distinct metabolic and spatial mechanisms. Disrupting glycogenolysis impairs tumor growth and mitochondrial pyruvate oxidation, compromises NADPH homeostasis, and selectively reduces glutamine utilization for reductive biosynthesis. Cytoplasmic and lysosomal glycogenolysis produce different defects in nucleotide precursor metabolism and distinct dependencies on biosynthetic enzymes. By contrast, disrupting glycogen synthesis creates a selective vulnerability to depletion of CAD, the multifunctional enzyme rate limiting for pyrimidine biosynthesis. Pyrimidine intermediates associate with glycogen particles, while glycogen availability influences their spatial distribution and the organization of the pyrimidine biosynthetic enzyme UMP synthase. Together, these findings identify glycogen as a source of biosynthetic substrates and a regulator of nucleotide metabolic organization, linking carbon storage and mobilization to cancer cell proliferation.

items.title: Real-world longitudinal multi-omics separates weight-loss-associated responses to incretin agonists from a broader response not dependent on weight loss
items.abstract: The benefits of incretin agonists, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, are largely attributed to glycemic control and weight loss, as these therapies enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release and delay gastric emptying to produce satiety. Yet treatment is also associated with lower risk of cardiometabolic, renal and other chronic diseases. Whether these broader benefits depend on weight loss itself or reflect direct effects of treatment on physiology remains unclear, as does the basis of the marked variation in how patients respond. Resolving these questions has been difficult because weight loss and drug effects occur together, and because molecular studies of treated patients have been limited in scope. Here we profiled paired plasma samples collected before and after treatment from 165 individuals drawn from DynamiQ, a biorepository that links plasma samples to longitudinal clinical records, combining mass spectrometry-based proteomics, a targeted inflammation proteomics panel (NULISAseq) and non-targeted metabolomics to capture metabolic function, inflammation and markers of chronic disease.
